p: Thank you. Sorry, Madam Chair. If I may have a few more questions. Thank you. During this construction process, can you speak about job retention on those who are currently there working? Will they be moved to another location to work or what will happen during the construction process? And can you talk about the implementation of new possible jobs being there after this is completed?

Yeah. So, the Hunts Point Food Dish Center has hundreds of jobs up there, thousands of jobs up there that are all mostly union, and all of those will be retained. Again, we're not closing anything. There's no businesses that are going to close temporarily. Everything is

going to be up and running all through the construction. In fact, there'll be tons of new construction jobs up there. Once it's fully online, then the produce market will move next door and it'll be fully operational. So, there'll be no time where people are out of work.

Okay. And my last set of questions will be focused on M/WBEs. Do you have… and I'm only asking this because I have a very interesting bill, not the place to speak about it, but I just want to know. Within my community, I have a lot of young people that are transitioning into entrepreneurship, right, and a lot of them want to learn about how to get City contracts. You spoke about 35 percent of the contracts were given to M/WBEs. Do you have like, I guess, an age range on those contracts given to those business owners between the ages of 18 and 25? And if you don't have that now, could you please provide that for me at some time? And also, would you guys be interested in entertaining the conversation of youth business entrepreneurship of guaranteeing these contracts to youth businesses?
We don't have that data, so we will have to get back to you on that, but we appreciate the question.
Okay. And would you guys be interested in that conversation with youth businesses?
We'd like to talk about it further. Yes. Thank you.
All right. Thank you so much. Thank you, Madam President. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member Riley. Turning to FIFA, one of the questions that Council Member Riley just brought up. I guess about a few weeks ago in our last hearing, we raised oversight over a lot of questions that have yet to be answered with FIFA, and the first match of the World Cup is just 86 days out. Do you have any more information that you can share about the World Cup-related plans, or I can get into more specific questions?

I mean, yes, we are working with the World Cup czar very closely and

sort of activating our sites for these engagements for the World Cup.
Great. Do we have any specifics on the programs or the partnerships that are in place to ensure small businesses are incorporated, and how will that support be measured?

Yeah. Again, we're working closely with the Mayor's Office on this. Also, you know, we have our own assets that we are going to activate, such as BAT, Coney Island, Staten Island, etc., Kingsbridge. So, our public markets are also a good venue. So, we are actively working with our asset management team to be making sure that we're going to activate that for community engagement and to support local small businesses.

In the oversight hearing, we heard from BIDs and community organizations about the plaza activation permit moratorium during and leading up to the World Cup, and has there been any progress made on lifting that moratorium from June 1st to July 18th so that BIDs can participate in fan activations and contribute to driving regional economic development and even just continue with their regularly scheduled programming?
I don't have that information, but we can look into that and get back to you on that.
And is EDC utilizing any additional funding outside of City Council allocations to support fan engagement and community events, for example, public-private partnerships?

Yes. You know, we have our own, like I said, our own budget. We're self-sustaining, so we'll be using our asset management budget that we have for our particular assets, and we are going to activate those assets for World Cup-related engagements using our own budget.
Great. Are there any other public-private partnerships in the works?
I'm not aware of this time.

In the scope of services contract, the projected economic output varies from 2.14 billion to 3.4 billion for what to expect from, in terms of local economic impact for the area. What steps is the City taking and EDC taking to ensure that our return is closer to the 3.4 billion?
This is for the World Cup?
For the World Cup.

We estimate about 3.3 billion of economic activity. Again, I think it's multiple sort of ways that we're going to create that activity. One is city residents just sort of being out, spending money, engaging. Visitors coming into the city, and also from other parts of the country, and also global delegations. Also, a lot of companies will be spending a lot of their own to create excitement and build upon the FIFA World Cup.

And then still within the World Cup, that 15 million in Fiscal Year 2026, is that going to be negotiated through an additional contract with the host committee, or spent separately? If you could share more information about that 15 million.
Yeah. Again, we're working with the World Cup czar now to see how it's going to be deployed and budgeted, and how it's going to be structured. So, we'll get back to you on that.

All right. We look forward to more information in 86 days. Just calling that out. I'm now going to ask Council Member Gutiérrez to ask questions, and then we'll turn to Shanel Thomas-Henry on Zoom. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you so much, Chair. And thank you all so much for your testimony. Before I ask questions, I just want to give flowers to the awesome folks at the Moore Street Market, at the Marqueta, Natalie, Eileen. It's been an amazing experience, really transformative. And so I'm really encouraged by your response to like what how these small businesses will be activated. Would love to, when the time comes, really learn a little bit more about it. But I just want to make sure that they get all the praise, because we're really happy and the community is really happy. My questions are, the first is just regarding industrial businesses. Council Member Farías and I in the last term worked really hard with DCP specifically on legislation to ensure thoughtful planning to preserve industrial businesses, as well

as, you know, creating opportunities for job retention. And so, I just have two questions related to one of their policies. The City just released its industrial plan late last year, calling for specialized place-based support for industrial businesses. And so my concern, and I think Council Member Farías' concern is about SBS' RFP that was released, essentially eliminating the industrial business service provider program and replacing it with a rotating borough-based model. So how does, and I get that this is a question for SBS and we will have that conversation, but you all at EDC, how do you think that a plan or an RFP like this really aligns with the recommendation of specialized place-based support for these industrial businesses? And you all are doing a tremendous amount of work.

Thank you for that question. You know, we greatly appreciated the Council's leadership in driving that industrial action plan. And, you know, we have a lot of City assets and they're focused on sort of industrial industries so, Brooklyn Army Terminal, Hunts Point that we talked about, Bathgate, East New York, one in three of our tenants are industrial companies, and

one out of 12 industrial companies in the outer boroughs are our tenants so we are really engaged with them. We are very focused on focusing on them, on the industrial sector and growing the industrial sector. And we are focused on workforce development and economically as it relates to those industrial sector. You know, again, we have the benefit of having Shehila Stephens here, so I'd like to turn it over to her to sort of answer any more additional color.

How are you? So, I do want to talk a little bit about EDC's commitment around equity, especially in these industrial industries. So, EDC launched what we call the East Brooklyn Fund in October 2025. So, this fund created opportunities to build capacity for community-based organizations. So, we spent a lot of time with the community, talking with them about like, what is the support that they need to be able to stay in place and grow, and this is really a part of our commitment to place-based equity. And so we did award over five community-based organizations to offer either workforce pipeline training, as well as transitioning from a workforce into an

entrepreneurship space, and also providing additional capacity for smaller industrial businesses to help them grow as well. So, we committed about 1.4 million to that particular fund. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Well, this is great. I remember hearing that in your testimony, but would it be too much to ask if you all connect with SBS and really speak to the thoughtfulness and success of this community-based program? It's really what the role of the industrial business service providers have been doing, have been funded in the city for the last 40 years to do. And every year they do come to these budget hearings and say, we need more money because we want to be able to do more of this work. And I really believe that this RFP is going to reverse a lot of that progress. And yes, you should have an unhappy face because we are out here really fighting for our industrial businesses, especially in Districts like ours that really employ such a vast majority of people. And you all know the benefits. I don't have to preach here to you, but it's really important that we really invest in organizations that are really filling holes for manufacturing businesses that are day-to-day facing

so many challenges, and we fought so hard in the, with the last Administration to make sure that we are being inclusive. So, I would love for some communication and maybe we can help make that happen. My next question is related to tech and I'll be fast. I see EDC is investing heavily in sectors like the green economy and energy infrastructure, yet many of those projects rely on industrial space and workforce. How is the City ensuring that industrial land and businesses are preserved as part of its broader tech and innovation strategy?

Yeah. So, tech is an important sector for New York City. It has diversified our economy here when we were like, you know, decades ago, very reliant on sort of the financial businesses. And now we've diversified so it's about 7 percent of our city's total workforce. We have about 25,000 tech-enabled startups. We're number two in the world in tech. And so we really are working hard to make sure that tech grows here. We understand though that there's a lot of communities that have been sort of boxed out of sort of the tech sector, and so we are working on creating workforce,

not only workforce, economic mobility programs, but also supporting diverse entrepreneurship through the Founder Fellowship program. COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: Yeah. I think they're both great. Thank you so much for highlighting it in your testimony. And please just keep the conversation going on that piece. And, Chair, can I just ask one more question? Related to childcare, there's a report that shows that EDC is investing hundreds of millions into economic development projects and long-term business incentives. How is the City thinking about childcare as part of its economic development strategy, particularly as a prerequisite for workforce participation?

Yeah. Affordable childcare is an incredibly important for the economic growth of the city. We understand that childcare is needed for all sort of workers to be able to go to their jobs and work every day, and so we are aligned with the Mayor on sort of figuring out sort of a childcare affordability solution. So, you know, we are working on that and we support that because it's part of economic development. It can't be separated.

COUNCIL MEMBER GUTIÉRREZ: And I'll just say last year, I want to also just uplift the work of the modular bathrooms. I think it's really great, really innovative, really excited for the administration. But I also just want to give flowers to my Colleagues, Council Member Joseph and Nurse who passed legislation on expanding bathroom access citywide before the Administration's announcement earlier this year and would just love more collaboration on some of these things, but really good stuff. Thank you so much, Chair.
Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. And now to Zoom, Council Member Thomas-Henry.

Thank you so much, Chair. Good afternoon, everyone. I have a couple of quick questions. In terms of, so Willard's Point is in my District, and I just wanted to get a timeline for Phase 2, so the rest of the affordable housing units, the school, the hotel.

Yes. So, we'll have to get back to you on the specific timeline. As you mentioned, Phase 2 includes additional 1,400 affordable units, a 25,000 privately financed all-electric soccer stadium, a 250-key hotel, about 115,000 additional square foot of open space, and more remediation on 17 acres there so, we are looking forward to that. We'll have to get back to you on a specific timeline.

Okay. And with that in mind, since that only accounts for about a third of the entire Willard's Point property, all that's out there, does the Admin have any desire, or have there been any conversations about acquiring additional parcels for affordable housing?
Well, part of the project includes a public school, and in order to build that public school, we do need to acquire some of those private assets, private sites. So, we are undergoing that right now.
But any discussions about the remaining approximately 40 acres that are out there privately, currently privately owned?
I'm not aware of that. I have to get back to you on that one.

Okay. Moving to ferry service. So, there is a desire by the community, the local electeds in the area, from the Borough President to our State electeds, to myself, for ferry service out at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park, the Malcolm X Promenade. Have any studies been done to see the feasibility of this? We have 880 units coming online next month, and right now there's only one bus that stops there and the 7 train, which on a good day is overcrowded, and then you have the soccer stadium opening next year, you have USTA, you have Citi Field. Have you guys started looking at the possibility of putting a ferry there?

Thank you so much for asking that question. We love talking about NYC ferries. We're really happy with our progress with NYC ferries. Everybody loves NYC ferries, and that's why everybody wants more NYC ferries in their communities. It's an important part of the transit hub of New York City, activating our waterways. You know, as I mentioned in my testimony, we're at an all-time high in ridership. 95 percent or over 90

percent of our riders are New York City residents, you know, students, senior citizens, commuters, and also we have these like fun services to the beach, Rockaway, Rocket, etc. So, we also have worked really, really, really hard to make it more efficient. So, our per-rider subsidy is the lowest it's ever been. In terms of expanded service, I'm going to turn it over to Josh Kraus, who runs the NYC ferry system.

Yeah. Thank you so much, Jeanny. So, you may have heard that towards the end of last year, we put out our 2025 Future of Ferries Report, and one of the things that was included within it was a vision for the future of ferry service, really across the harbor. We are deeply aware of the interest that many communities have in seeing expansion of the NYC ferry service, and through this study, this is going to be the vehicle for us to really take an in-depth look at some of these places that have long been called for, such as the one at Willett's Point that you raise, and delve deeply into understanding all of the constraints and opportunities that may exist. So, we

are just getting started on that study, and as we proceed with it, we're going to be working very, very closely with communities, with Council Members, with affected stakeholders, and all who have jurisdiction to help us really evaluate the possibility of going farther than we have before. And I'll even point out that really, even within the Ferry Report that we put out last year, Willett's Point is one of the locations that we flagged for study, so we are definitely aware of it, and we're looking forward to getting that work started.

And just to plug, it would be great if you tested it out during FIFA. We have one of the fan zones right here in our backyard, and we also have the Mets playing for a good length of time that it's here, so that would be a perfect opportunity to test it out. Another quick question, with the Sunnyside project, with federal funds being involved, would that rely on the federal DBE program in terms of participation, or would we still be able to rely on our M/WBE program for participation on construction opportunities for that plan?

Yeah. The Sunnyside Yard redevelopment is sort of a generational development to bring over, you know, 100 acres, creating tons of housing, open space, commercial uses, etc. The visit from the Mayor to Washington with the 21-billion-dollar price tag is sort of the initial conversation, allowing us to have conversations with our federal, state, and local partners, and engaging the community in sort of everything in the development. As you know, NYCEDC developed the Sunnyside Yard Master Plan in 2020, so we are now sort of in the initial conversation, so we'll know more as time goes on.

I do want to flag for you, if it is dependent upon the DBE program, as of last year, the Trump Administration has rescinded a lot of those certifications based on gender and race, so a lot of our firms that were certified under the DBE certification program have to be recertified, so as any conversations are being had, it would be good to keep that in mind, because it would be a great disadvantage that a lot of our women and minority businesses don't get to partake in this monumental development.
Thank you. We appreciate that comment. We'll take note.

My final question, Chair, if I may, with the 250th anniversary, similar to the World Cup, is there a plan in terms of promoting it, revenue generating activities, merchandise, or the like, to help the City?
Yeah. We're very excited for Sail 250. We are activating our waterways for that, and I'm going to turn it over to Anton.

Thank you for the question. So, 250th birthday of the United States. We're estimating 2.85 billion dollars of economic impact as part of that, so this is July 3rd to 9th, we'll be welcoming 46 nations, 50 tall ships, and 52 allied and U.S. naval vessels, and EDC is supporting in accommodating those vessels to the New York Harbor, so we're really looking forward to that event.
Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member Thomas-Henry.

On the World Cup, one final question, the Comptroller and Council Finance estimates a 50 million dollar return for the City in tax revenue. Can EDC share any estimates that they have generated for local tax revenue?
In terms of the FIFA World Cup, we've not done our own projection from what I'm aware of.

And building on our favorite topic, the New York City Ferry, I personally love riding the ferry, I know we have new local laws to make it easier and more affordable for middle school students to take the ferry approximately one month from now. What increase in ridership do you expect after those laws go into place?

Thank you so much for the question, and we share your excitement. It's been since September of 2024 that we've been welcoming our high school students on board, and this has been a really successful program, very meaningful for those high schoolers who are able to now commute by ferry, and we're very excited to now do the same for our middle schoolers. We intend to follow a similar playbook in terms of getting the

word out, working with our partners of the Department of Education, working with our operator, Hornblower, through their social media, through our social media, doing tabling, doing everything we can to make sure that we get the greatest possible uptick in ridership there. We don't have any projections right now, but we are really looking forward to welcoming our middle schoolers on board.

That's great. And I want to again commend you on ridership trending upward, reaching a record high of 7.4 million in Fiscal Year 2025, and subsidy per rider trending down to roughly 8 dollars in Fiscal Year 2025. What steps is EDC taking to continue to increase ridership and lower that cost per rider subsidy?

Thank you so much for highlighting the work that we have been so focused on over the past four years, especially through our NYC Ferry Forward program. As you correctly point out, we are now at record high ridership coupled with record low subsidy per rider, and we don't intend on looking back.

So, I'll talk about probably two things that come to mind first when it comes to making sure that our ridership remains robust and that we are welcoming as many New Yorkers as possible onto our boats. The first one is the work that we really talked a lot about and began towards the end of last year, which was to really reconfigure the routes that we have in NYC Ferry. The things that we did, a couple of the most important ones, were one, to break our very, very popular East River route into an A route and a B route, which we did to ensure that we would have faster travel times and fewer folks who are left behind. We also, for the first time in many, many decades, re-established a water-based transportation between Staten Island and Brooklyn. I remember the tremendous excitement, despite the frigid weather that we had on the day that it was begun. And so even beyond that, we've also made some small changes to ensure that more riders across the system have access to Midtown, and the reason we did that is because in the surveys that we completed leading up to our change, that's one of the main things we heard, is that our riders, especially our regular riders, are seeking opportunities for

employment, for healthcare, for entertainment in Midtown, and we want to be responsive to that request to those riders. That's why I think when we got our surveys back, the tremendous majority, something like 90 percent, said that on the basis of what we are doing, they would ride the same or more, so we have had that in place since December, and we're just now starting to really see, as we get into the warmer months, how successful that's going to be. Our prediction is that thanks to this reconfigured route system, we're going to see even more riders, so that's a very big piece of how we are moving the system forward and ensuring continued ridership. The other thing that we did is to create a new ticket. We created a new ticket type, mostly targeted at tourists, but also for New Yorkers who want to do some intensive ferry riding over a two-day period, so this too, a two-day unlimited 15-dollar ticket, we think is going to help us to reach more people. It's a great deal for riders. It's a great deal for us, so these are just a couple of the ways that we are not resting on our laurels and continuing to drive ridership on NYC Ferry.
Thank you. I raise my hand as interested in the two-day unlimited ticket.
All right.
As you're thinking about new… well, first off, when are those new routes to be implemented?
So, they are going on now.
Okay.
They have been implemented.
And have you seen any shifts in ridership or any data changes?

So, there's a reason why we made this change in the December time period. It's because this is generally among the lower sort of ridership times of year, and the good thing about that is that it allows our riders, and in fact even our system operator, to develop a rhythm and to really perfect the way the schedules are working before we get to the spring and summer months when ridership is really high. So, it's

probably a little too early to draw meaningful conclusions from the data, but from what we have seen so far, we're seeing a small but measurable uptick in ridership, especially on our East River route and our St. George route.

That's encouraging. And as you're looking at new ferry terminal sites, in new neighborhoods like Council Member Shanel Thomas-Henry mentioned, how do you measure whether expansion will generate sufficient ridership to open up that site or other economic or social returns that justify the investment?

Excellent question. Thank you so much. This is we spend a lot of time focused on. There are a number of factors, one of which is the ability for the service to really work from a physical and operational standpoint. Not all areas in our waterfront are exactly the same in terms of water depth, in terms of access. So, we need to make sure that at a minimum, the physical access and the operational accessibility are there. Then we also look at whether the service that we provide can be competitive with other modes that are existing options for riders. So, if there is

a subway ride that can be substantially faster than the service that we can offer, we think it might be less likely that we're going to have a huge amount of ridership, even though sometimes there are mitigating factors because people say they enjoy the commute so much more. We also take a very close look at the upland conditions, so to speak, how easy it is for members of a community, folks in the neighborhood to access the landing, and also we look at socioeconomic and demographic factors. It is very important to us that NYC Ferry is accessible to all New Yorkers from all walks of life. So, this is something that is really centered in our evaluation and is something that we're going to be taking a very close look at in the vision study that I talked about earlier.

Thank you. One last question. The Preliminary Plan includes 4 million in FY26 of federal Highway Administration grant funding. How can EDC maximize incoming funds from those types of grants? Is it based on ridership? What are the other factors?

Thank you so much. We're looking at that as well. Obviously, we want to maximize the amount of federal

dollars that we get. Some of them are earmarks. Some of them are formula based. So, we're going to continue to look at all of the federal opportunities and do what we can to maximize those.
Would expanding to more locations, particularly other boroughs that aren't served by ferry access right now, would that unlock additional funds or not necessarily?
I'd have to look a little bit more carefully at the language of some of the federal bills and get back to you on that question.
Thank you. I'm going to now turn to Council Member Banks. And I also want to recognize that we have Council Member Avilés who joined us, and I'll turn to her afterwards for questions.

Thank you, Madam Chair. First of all, I heard East New York mentioned a couple of times so it's always good to hear that.

Particularly, and I guess on a sidebar, I would love to hear about the plan on how they're going to activate the community for the World Cup. I know that was mentioned, that you're going to activate the East New York community so we'd definitely love to have further conversation about that, as well as we would love to get a timeframe on the BRC, 160-million-dollar project that is supposed to be a demolition, and we're supposed to get a new community center so, if we can get some information on that particular timeframe on that as well. Also, too, in our District, we also do have a desire for a ferry service as well. As you do know, we're right up the block from the Canarsie Pairs, and we do have the amazing Shirley Chisholm Park that definitely a lot of residents would be happy if there was a ferry service, especially in that area where there is a transportation desert in the Starrett City, the more southern part of my District. Let me get to my line of questions, particularly dealing with the energy storage community impact. Given the concentration of energy storage projects and ongoing concerns from residents, what resources in the 2027 preliminary budget are

being allocated for community engagement, oversight, and safety view of these developments?

Yeah. Thank you for that question. The battery storage projects are incentivized through our IDA benefits. So, these are private companies that come in that we structure these transactions individually so that they provide tax incentives for them to build battery storage, which is incredibly important for our green economy and building a more resilient New York City. It does have benefits to the community because it takes off these gaseous peaker plants that put out noxious fumes into the community to a more greener sort of renewable energy grid. So, this is an IDA program, and through that, in each of the battery storage projects that we've done recently, we've ensured that there's a workforce development component that these companies are creating to train local residents to serve in this new industry of battery storage. And so, it's not only just at the plant, but all these companies have relocated and built their offices in New York City, in Brooklyn, and so their headquarters was not quoted in sort of the jobs created by the IDA

project, but they are creating jobs in that company for Brooklyn residents.

All right. And I guess you'd probably answer this, but I'm going to ask the question, is the EDC currently involved or supporting the proposed battery storage project in the Jewel Street area? And if so, what outreach has been conducted with residents in the 42nd Council District? And additionally, what resources are being directed specifically to my District to ensure meaningful community engagement?
Yeah. So, I'll have to check specifically about Jewel Street, if it's an IDA project or not, and so we'll get back to you on that.

If you can. When it comes down to Brooklyn's EDC support, in the last year's preliminary budget, Brooklyn received approximately 12.1 million in economic development support and about 709 million in lifetime support, the second lowest among the boroughs, despite being the largest borough by population. How does the FY27 preliminary budget address this imbalance?
You know, I'd have to get back to you on that. I don't have the specifics on sort of that budget now. I'm not sure.
If you can get back to me, I'd appreciate that. Can you provide any updated figures or anything? Is there any information that you have?
I am not sure that goes through EDC specifically, but we'll get back to you.

Okay. Also, when it comes down to small business support that we believe has taken a decline based off the data, the data shows that the number of small businesses served declined by 8 percent from over 6,000 to just over 5,500. Yet there were no new investments in the 2027 preliminary budget to address this. Why is small business support declining, and are there any resources to reverse this trend?

Yeah. So, EDC focuses on sort of supporting small businesses through our assets. Again, we have 64 million square feet, 224 assets, and primarily it's Brooklyn Army Terminal, Hunts Point, East New York, Coney Island,

etc., and also our public markets, you know, we have three major public markets. One is Moore Street in Brooklyn, and so, through that, we support small businesses. We also support small businesses, M/WBE businesses through our sort of construction awards. So, 35 percent of all of our construction awards are to M/WBE. That equates to about 240 million last year. And we have sort of pathways to break barriers of entry for M/WBE firms, both in sort of maritime construction and also regular construction through our Construct NYC and Waterfront Pathways Program.

Okay. Thank you for that response. I have two more questions, if you may, endorse, Madam Chair. Since we just spoke about M/WBE participation, we're going to talk about the decline. M/WBE participation has declined significantly from over 40 percent to under 20 percent. What specific funding and corrective actions are included in the FY27 preliminary budget to reverse this trend and how will the Administration ensure accountability and meeting participation goals?

So, the City has a 30 percent M/WBE goal. EDC on our projects that we manage and we award, we have a 35 percent M/WBE goal, and we have been meeting that. We met that in last year, as I mentioned in Fiscal '25, and we anticipate meeting that 35 percent goal in Fiscal '26.

And the last thing, we want to also, you know, thank the EDC for the East Brooklyn work workforce fund. The 42nd Council District had the opportunity to partake in it. We had two community-based organizations that were recipients of the RFP or selected, so we thank you for that opportunity. Obviously, it's still in effect because they're doing the work so we want to thank you for that and, you know, the participation in that as well. Thank you, Madam Chair.
Thank you. We really appreciate that.

Council Member Avilés. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you, Chair.

Hello, friends. I know you're waiting for me. I need more time, of course, but let me not belabor the many, many questions I have. So, I guess first I want to underscore the importance of Council Member Gutiérrez's comment about the change of the RFP related to industrial businesses and our profound concerns there. Could you tell me what metrics EDC uses to track industrial growth? And is there a metric that you are using on a yearly basis to note whether in fact that is happening?

Yeah. So, our assets are very industrial focused. We have one in three of our tenants at our assets are industrial companies and one in 12 of the industrial companies in outer boroughs are at our assets. So, we invest heavily not only in sort of as tenants, but as an industry. So, we are constantly looking at how to support the industrial sector, both in the new development projects, as well as in our existing assets. And so we know it's a very important workforce for, you know, high paying good jobs for blue collar workers, and so it's really important to

us to make sure that that industry expands, is supported and grows. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Right. So can you I guess off the record, if you would send me what the breakdown of those industries are and the markers.

Sure. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Having one in three tenants necessarily doesn't say that we are meeting growth targets. It means that's what's existing. Are we maintaining those and what is in fact the growth target, and are we pushing those targets, you know, in the coming years? So, I'd love to really learn more granularly how growth is defined and whether or not we are actually meeting that in the various sectors, because I'm sure there are smaller manufacturers, larger, and what we consider industrial might be a point of, I don't know, interpretation.

Yes. Thank you. We'll reach out to you. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yeah. So, in terms of has, can EDC provide its gross and net revenues for the last Fiscal Years, like for Fiscal '25 or Fiscal '24, '25, and '26.

Yeah. So, so EDC is a not-for-profit organization and we collect, operate, and maintain assets on behalf of the City. criteria in place such as income levels or food insecurity rates or retail gaps that are being used to determine the locations?
